source: CARDI (2011), "Handbook of Integrated Techniques for Increasing Wet-Season and Dry-Season Rice Productivity" (Khmer, 50pp, funded by CAVAC/ACIAR, foreword by H.E. Chan Sarun, Minister of Agriculture, dated 26 August 2011)
text: A good seedbed (thnal samnab) gives even, healthy seedling growth for transplanting. Site selection: choose a spot near a reliable water source that is easy to visit and monitor, and away from streetlights, since light at night attracts insect pests that damage seedbeds. It helps to keep a small reserve of stored water next to the seedbed for irrigating during a dry spell. Area needed: about 10 m² of seedbed per kilogram of seed to be sown (so roughly 200–300 m² of seedbed per hectare of field, for the usual 20–30 kg/ha broadcasting rate); a 1 kg seed lot needs at least 1 are (100 m²) if instead being used to raise transplants for 1 hectare at a 20 kg/ha rate (this is the same area guidance used for the seed-purification nursery). Bed preparation: plow the seedbed site at least 3 times so old weed seed and shattered rice grain from a previous crop are killed and cannot contaminate the new seedlings — first plowing turns the soil and buries the first flush of weeds/volunteer rice after 5–10 cm of seedling growth has appeared following the first rain; second plowing 10–15 days before sowing turns under whatever weeds/volunteer rice grew back; a third plowing just 1–3 days before sowing (and at least 3 days if there was a lot of weed growth) lets any remaining weeds rot down before sowing. Rake/clear away crop residue before final leveling and make the seedbed surface smooth and even. Lay out seedbeds in strips about 2 m wide to make it easy to walk between them for monitoring. Sowing: soak seed in warm water for 2–3 hours before sowing and skim off and discard any grains that float, since floaters are typically less viable or hollow. Divide the seed evenly across all bed sections and sow evenly by hand. Care: watch the seedbed daily, especially for the first week, for insect pests (particularly crickets/armyworm-type pests) and weeds; if the seedbed has had little or no rain for more than a week, it must be inspected for pest damage. Nursery age at transplanting: non-photoperiod-sensitive/light varieties should not be transplanted after more than 20 days in the nursery; medium- and heavy/photoperiod-sensitive varieties can go 25–30 days. Water shortage for transplanting the main wet-season crop is a frequent cause of farmers delaying transplanting, which can leave medium and heavy varieties in the nursery for up to 3 months; delaying transplanting still gives an acceptable yield as long as the time from transplanting to panicle initiation is at least 1 month, but if that window drops to 1 week or less, farmers should not transplant that seedling stock at all — they should instead consider it only usable for broadcasting, since the crop will not be able to produce a full yield in the time remaining.
